https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases.text: Drive-side force sensing and a 1:1 motion-mimicking interface make every procedure a training-grade record of expert clinical skill KAUNAS, Lithuania , July 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sentante , the medical robotics company building a haptic, device-agnostic platform for remote vascular surgery, is turning its newly CE-marked robotic system into a data engine for the next generation of intelligent, endovascular intervention. Much of the field claims autonomy ahead of the data needed to deliver it. Sentante built the opposite: a system architected from the start to capture force and torque, device kinematics and time-aligned fluoroscopy together, on every procedure. Hardware and AI are one effort, and each procedure refines the dataset that makes increasing machine assistance possible. "The next wave of technology is physical AI: systems that can sense, act and operate in the real world, not just process information," said Edvardas Satkauskas, CEO and co-founder of Sentante. "For endovascular intervention, the constraint has never been ambition, it has been data. You cannot train a system to navigate a living vessel without a rich, accurate record of how the best clinicians do it. We have spent years building the platform that captures exactly that, and CE mark means it is now generating that data in real clinical settings across Europe." Imaging is being deliberately reduced, and force has to fill the gap: Fluoroscopy and contrast media both carry harm: radiation exposure for patients and staff, and contrast-related risk, notably renal injury. Guidelines accordingly push every endovascular procedure toward minimum imaging, which means the situational-awareness data available to the operator goes down, not up. The hand fills the gap: the load profile up the catheter column distinguishes safe contact from a perforation precursor. On a dose-limited 2D image the two can look identical, and no computer-vision force indicator can recover a signal that was never captured. An AI built on imaging alone is extracting more from a data source the field is deliberately driving down. Drive-side force and torque sensing remains rare in medical robotics; da Vinci 5 only brought force feedback to laparoscopy in March 2024, with preclinical evidence of up to 43% less force on tissue . Sentante engineered force and torque sensing into the catheter drive from day one, and the endovascular setting makes the case even stronger: a thin column of wire and catheters in continuous contact with the vessel wall, where the safety envelope is a load profile, not a position. "The image tells you where the device is. The hand tells you what the vessel is doing," said Dr. Tomas Baltrūnas, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Sentante. "A system that captures only the image is missing the half that matters most for safety." The interface decides whether the data carries real skill: Every joystick or screen-based controller in endovascular robotics forces the operator to translate a career of feel and micro-adjustment through an artificial input layer. The captured demonstration records expert joystick operation, not expert catheter operation, and the demonstrator pool is limited to physicians who have completed a months-long learning curve on that specific robot. Sentante's platform is different: the clinician manipulates standard catheters and guidewires exactly as in manual intervention, with authentic force feedback at the fingertips, and the system records that natural motor program directly. The captured behaviour carries the actual clinical skill, the demonstrator pool expands to every existing interventionalist, and every procedure performed on the platform is a training-grade demonstration in its natural form. Da Vinci proved the principle in 1999: its one-to-one motion-mimicking console let manual surgical skill transfer without re-learning, and that made it adoptable. Sentante applies the same logic to the catheter, removing the training-bandwidth bottleneck of every prior platform: an expert is competent from day one, and the system accumulates training data from day one. "What I learned to do with my hands over fifteen years of intervention is replicable with the Sentante platform." said Baltrūnas . "The motion-mimicking interface lets me operate as I always have, with the platform recording what I do as I do it. The expertise stays in the operator's hands, and the data stays in the system." Over the past year the company has run a world-first transatlantic remote thrombectomy on perfused human cadaver models and a GLP animal study of 24 remote procedures across three continents, each adding to a dataset built under procedure-authentic conditions. The CE-marked system integrates with existing cath-lab infrastructure and supports peripheral vascular interventions, with remote stroke thrombectomy on a parallel regulatory pathway. The latest-generation robot uses NVIDIA hardware, and Sentante was among the first to develop on NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare. Sentante is continuing its European commercial rollout, progressively introducing AI-driven assistance as the dataset matures. About Sentante: Sentante is a medical robotics company founded in 2017 building a haptic, device-agnostic endovascular platform that enables clinicians to perform complex vascular procedures remotely with full tactile feedback. Designed to integrate with existing cath-lab infrastructure, Sentante aims to expand access, improve clinician safety, and elevate procedural consistency across peripheral vascular, neurovascular and cardiovascular applications. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago. Photograph: RichardBaker/Alamy View image in fullscreen The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago. Photograph: RichardBaker/Alamy Economics UK graduate job vacancies plunge to lowest in a decade Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, says recruitment website Adzuna Business live – latest updates Alex Daniel Mon 24 Aug 2026 02.55 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 05.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Graduate job vacancies in the UK have sunk to their lowest level since they started being tracked a decade ago, according to a recruiting website. Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, Adzuna reported on Monday, down 45% compared with the same point last year and the lowest since the company started gathering the data in 2016. The number comes as 262,820 people prepare to go to university in September, a record high that underlines the tough conditions facing graduates entering the job market as entry-level roles are threatened by AI . UK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank finds Read more About 1 million young people in the UK were not in education, employment or training, otherwise known as Neets, in the first quarter of this year, according to the Office for National Statistics. Adzuna said sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies, adding that the figures suggested that a recovery reported during the spring had gone into reverse. Andrew Hunter, a co-founder of Adzuna, said: “July’s numbers are a step backwards, not a blip. The annual vacancy decline got worse for the first time since January, and (the number of) jobseekers per vacancy are now higher than they were a year ago. “The graduate job market also keeps setting new lows, which tells us employers still haven’t found a reason to open up hiring at that level.” The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago. In 2017, there were more than 55,000 graduate positions. More recently, employers have also reined in their hiring in the face of increases in national insurance contributions and the minimum wage announced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in her last two budgets. The extra labour cost for businesses also comes as some companies are prioritising investment in automation and artificial intelligence tools rather than hiring. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The trend has left some young people increasingly demoralised . One report, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), said this summer that 16- to 21-year-olds were less confident about being successful than a decade ago and that some were “losing faith in their futures”. In July, Andy Burnham said he would try to boost youth employment with more backing for technical education and apprenticeships . The only sectors showing increases in jobs for university leavers were travel, teaching and construction, Adzuna said. Hunter added: “It isn’t all bad news. Teaching, travel, and trade and construction are still adding roles, and manufacturing is now doing the same, too. But that’s a short list, and everyone outside of these sectors is having a harder time than they were three months ago.” Explore more on these topics Economics Graduate careers Work & careers UK unemployment and employment statistics Students Higher education news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UK employers cut job vacancies as Burnham aims to lift living standards Britain’s markets attracting generation of highly educated entrepreneurs Record number of young people fear long-term unemployment Number of young people out of work or training in UK could hit 1.25m by early 2030s Next boss warns over ‘dramatic fall’ in UK entry-level jobs Labour needs ‘system reset’ to tackle youth unemployment, report to say UK has wealthy Europe’s ‘third-highest’ rate of young adults not in work or study UK pay growth sinks to five-year low as younger workers hit by hiring slowdown UK job vacancies ‘fall to lowest level since pandemic’ Number of employed people in UK falls again as wage growth slows Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://www.cubaheadlines.com/articles/3.text: Marco Rubio Warns Cuban Change Won't Happen "Overnight" Wednesday, August 12, 2026 by Zoe Salinas On Tuesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed confidence that Cuba will be on an "irreversible path toward a very different future" before the end of the Trump administration. However, he cautioned that this transformation won't occur immediately. Rubio made these remarks during episode 51 of the "Katie Miller Pod" podcast, recorded at the State Department alongside his wife, Jeanette. "You can't have something in place for 70 years, deeply rooted, and expect to uproot it overnight and replace it with something new. There's a transition that must happen and a process to get there," the Secretary of State explained. Lessons from Eastern Europe To provide context, Rubio referenced the recent history of Eastern Europe as an example. "Eastern Europe offers a lesson in this regard. It took Eastern European countries between three to five years to truly become what we recognize today. Poland is probably the best example," he noted. The U.S. chief diplomat emphasized that Cuba is a priority for the Trump administration due to national interest, not just personal ties to the island. "I work for the United States. I care about Cuba. Obviously, I have a personal connection, but I don't work for Cuba. I work for the U.S., and it's in our national interest to have a secure, stable, and U.S.-aligned Cuba," Rubio declared. A Persistent Critic of Havana As the son of Cuban immigrants who arrived in the United States in 1956, Rubio has been one of the most vocal critics of the Havana regime, a stance he has maintained since becoming Secretary of State. The podcast statements reinforce a message Rubio had delivered days earlier. On August 7, he revealed in an Axios interview the strategy of "closing every escape mechanism" for the Cuban government, and on the same day, he set the goal of placing Cuba on an "irreversible trajectory" by the end of the administration. Since January 2026, the Trump administration has taken more than two dozen actions against the Cuban regime, imposing sanctions on over 40 entities and at least 38 individuals linked to organizations like GAESA and CUPET . In July, Rubio had already dismissed the idea that Washington had a public timeline for regime change, although he expressed hope it would happen "tomorrow." His reference to Poland as a model for a three-to-five-year transition suggests the administration is managing medium-term expectations rather than immediate impacts. "It's certainly a priority for us because it's in our national interest. I never guarantee anything, but it's certainly a priority," Rubio concluded, extending the same objective to Venezuela : that both countries become "secure, stable, and aligned with the U.S." Understanding U.S. Policy Towards Cuba What is Marco Rubio's stance on Cuba? Marco Rubio is a longstanding critic of the Cuban regime. He emphasizes that the U.S. should work toward a secure, stable, and U.S.-aligned Cuba, which is in the national interest. Why does Rubio compare Cuba's situation to Eastern Europe? Rubio uses Eastern Europe as a reference to illustrate that significant transitions can take years, as it happened with countries like Poland, which took three to five years to stabilize and align with Western ideals. What actions has the Trump administration taken against Cuba? Since January 2026, the Trump administration has sanctioned over 40 entities and 38 individuals connected to Cuban structures such as GAESA and CUPET, as part of its strategy against the Cuban regime. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ukraine-w.text: Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Updated Fri, August 21, 2026 at 7:11 AM UTC 0 People at a rally in support of Mykhailo Fedorov outside the Ukrainian parliament on Wednesday. The protests’ organiser, Dmytro Koziatynskyi, appeared to call them off after Fedorov called for wartime elections.Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock The leader of weeks of protests against Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s sacking of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister appeared to call them off after Fedorov demanded elections. The pro-Fedorov movement’s chief ‌organiser, veteran combat medic Dmytro Koziatynskyi, said he “cannot imagine” how to hold polls with troops at the front and the protests had been about seeking dialogue with the government. Elections are considered impossible and illegal under Ukrainian law because of the war. “I’m also deeply concerned about the societal divisions during the election process and how that could affect the course of the war,” Koziatynskyi said. “In any case, street protests are definitely not the place for electoral discourse .” The Reuters news agency said that on Wednesday only a few dozen people remained in a central Kyiv square where thousands once protested. “When we came out to protest, we did not come with the idea that elections should be held,” said 22-year-old Iryna Vasyliaka. “That is ⁠not what we were here for.” Fedorov’s call for elections appeared to be a clumsy misstep , one opposition lawmaker told Reuters. “This demonstrates that [Fedorov] doesn’t have a presidential-level feel for the country.” Olena Prokopenko from the German Marshall Fund said Fedorov’s move was a “false start” that could burn his political ​capital before elections would realistically be held. “With this statement, he pretty much played on Ukrainians’ most sensitive pain points.” Ukraine’s parliament this week strongly endorsed Zelenskyy’s new defence minister and Fedorov’s successor, Yevhenii Khmara; but the protests did force Ukraine’s president to replace Oleksandr Syrskyi , the disliked “Soviet-style” head of Ukraine’s military, with a younger military reformer, Mykhailo Drapatyi . A Russian-Australian man has been arrested for allegedly passing information on Ukrainian military activity to Russian intelligence . The Australian federal police (AFP) arrested the man, 27, on Thursday night in the Australian city of Brisbane, charging him with attempting to engage in foreign interference. Commissioner Krissy Barrett of the AFP said it was alleged the man travelled to Russia in October 2024 for military-style training before returning to Australia and keeping in contact with “individuals he believed were connected to Russian intelligence services”. “Investigators will allege the man then travelled to Ukraine in May 2025, where he joined the Ukrainian armed forces , gaining access to information relating to military personnel, units, and locations.” Information was then passed on to Russia, Barrett said. Ukraine reeled on Thursday from a heavy Russian missile and drone bombardment that killed at least 16 people in and around Kyiv in one of the most intense aerial attacks on Ukraine’s capital since the start of the war. Vitali Klitschko, the city’s mayor, said homes, a school and a children’s medical centre were among the buildings damaged in an attack that began at about midnight and continued throughout the day. Volodymr Zelenskyy urged a global response to the attacks. “While Moscow is investing in ballistic missiles and escalation, such strikes do not always receive the response they should. And as long as Ukraine does not have enough anti-ballistic defence, Russia will not consider peace seriously .” A Romanian F-16 fighter jet on Thursday destroyed an explosives-laden Russian marine drone near an offshore gas project. “I strongly condemn the escalation of such irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation,” said the Romanian president, Nicușor Dan. The drone had been “loaded with explosives” and did not originate from Ukraine, said Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță. Hundreds of people are working at the gas project, Neptun Deep, according to Romania’s government. Neptun Deep is due to start production in 2027. Nato has shot down four aerial drones in Romania recently. Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission chief, slammed the “hybrid warfare” campaign by Russia against the EU after the marine drone incident. “An escalating campaign of threats is under way, unsettling our citizens and seeking to divide our union,” von der Leyen said, warning the EU must step up its defence push to be able to “deter provocation and aggression”. Poland on Thursday announced the arrest of a Ukrainian man suspected of an attempt in Kyiv to assassinate a representative of Ukraine’s arms industry on behalf of Russian intelligence services . “The investigation revealed that Serhii P planted an improvised explosive device under a car used by a potential victim,” said Poland’s internal security agency, the ABW. “The device was intended to be detonated ‌remotely using a cellphone. The mechanism did not detonate due to a malfunction.” The suspect fled to Poland where he was arrested in Warsaw. He was charged with attempted murder using explosives and illegal possession of explosives. Ukraine’s ⁠military hit ⁠Russia’s Taneco ⁠oil refinery ​in the Tatarstan ⁠region, as well ⁠as ​the Tamanneftegaz ‌oil terminal ‌in the ‌Krasnodar region , the Ukrainian General Staff said on ‌Thursday. The strikes caused fires ​at both ​sites. Disgruntled motorists in Moscow are sitting for hours in gasoline station queues of up to a kilometres to fill their cars with rationed amounts of fuel , Reuters reported. Videos showed fistfights erupting at the pumps , as Vladimir Putin’s regime reportedly ordered that people who complain about the shortages face fines and arrest . “We have been to five petrol stations already and there was no fuel. ‌Last week, fuel was available. And now, there is no fuel again,” one Moscow resident told Reuters. Russia attacked ⁠ gas infrastructure in Ukraine’s northern ⁠Chernihiv ⁠region as ​well as a border ⁠crossing with Moldova in the ⁠southern Odesa region, ​ ‌Volodymyr Zelenskyy ‌said.
